name: Kinesiology tape posture taping

card.summary: Elastic tape across the upper back as a shoulder-position reminder; the tape's pain evidence is thin and posture-for-looks is untested.
card.note: No studies found on taping for posture or appearance.

quick.overview:
Posture taping means sticking elastic kinesiology tape across the shoulders and upper back so that you feel a tug when your shoulders slump. Some people use it hoping for a straighter, more open posture.
The tape was developed in the 1970s and became famous at the Olympics. Reviews of it for pain and performance report small effects, and no study among those found tests it for posture appearance.
quick.mechanism: The idea is sensory feedback: the tape pulls on the skin when posture slips, which proponents say improves body awareness. Manufacturers have also claimed effects on fascia and lymph flow, which critics say lack evidence.
quick.risks: Reported risks are minor; skin irritation from adhesive is a general consideration. In 2017 the leading brand settled a lawsuit over marketing claims.

lead: Kinesiology tape posture taping is the use of stretchy, adhesive elastic tape, commonly sold as Kinesio tape or K-tape, across the shoulders and upper back to cue a more upright shoulder position. People use it to counter rounded shoulders and forward-head posture, which they associate with a broader-looking upper body, a more open chest and a cleaner side profile and neck line.[1]

The tape is a thin cotton strip with acrylic adhesive that can stretch to roughly 140 percent of its length. It was developed in the 1970s by Kenzo Kase, a Japanese-American chiropractor, and became widely visible after it was supplied to athletes at the 2008 and 2012 Olympics.[1]

Unlike most uses of the tape, posture taping has been studied directly. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine randomized trials with 293 participants found that taping groups differed significantly from controls on forward shoulder angle but not on craniovertebral angle or pain, and the authors noted that the evidence quality is low.[2] A 2024 double-blind trial in 114 people with rounded shoulders and shoulder impingement reported posture improvements over sham taping immediately after application.[3]

angle.text: Users apply strips across the shoulder blades so that the tape tugs on the skin when the shoulders slump, serving as a reminder to hold them back. Trials have measured forward shoulder angle, with a meta-analysis reporting a difference from control groups.[2]

paras: Kinesiology tape is a latex-free elastic cotton tape with a heat-activated acrylic adhesive, designed to approximate the thickness and elasticity of skin. When applied under stretch it recoils and tugs gently on the skin.[1]

For posture, practitioners and users apply strips across the upper back or shoulder blades so that the tape tension is felt when the shoulders round forward, intended as a sensory reminder rather than a mechanical brace.

Kenzo Kase developed the tape in the 1970s and his company sells it under the Kinesio brand. Its popularity rose after the product was donated to athletes at the 2008 Beijing and 2012 London Olympics, and beach volleyball player Kerri Walsh wearing it on her shoulder in 2008 is often cited as a visible moment.[1]

In 2017 the company KT Health settled a Massachusetts class action over its marketing for 1.75 million US dollars, agreeing to refunds and to drop claims such as injury prevention while adding a disclaimer that the tape was not clinically proven for all injuries.[1]

Manufacturers and users have proposed that the tape lifts the skin to decompress fascia, improves lymphatic flow, reduces pressure on pain receptors, or improves proprioception, meaning the awareness of body position. Critics cited by Wikipedia say these claims lack supporting evidence.[1] The proprioception-cue explanation is the one most aligned with posture use.

Posture taping applies strips across the upper back or shoulder blades so that the skin is tugged when the shoulders round forward. Users describe the cue as helping them hold the shoulders back through the day, and the look they aim for is a more open chest and a straighter neck line.[1]

The distinction researchers draw is between a sensory cue and a structural change: the trials above measure posture while the tape is on or shortly after application, and the 2024 trial states it examined immediate effects only.[2][3] Posture outcomes after the tape is removed have not been the focus of published trials.

Reviews of the tape across all uses are summarised on Wikipedia. A 2012 meta-analysis by Williams and colleagues in Sports Medicine reported trivial pain relief and little quality evidence that Kinesio tape differs from other elastic tapes in sports injuries; a 2014 meta-analysis by Csapo and Alegre found negligible effects on muscle strength and noted that lower-quality studies were more likely to report benefits.[1]

Commentators writing in Science-Based Medicine (Steven Novella in 2012, Clay Jones in 2018) and the Skeptoid writer Brian Dunning (2012) have criticised the proposed mechanisms and the tape's visibility at the Olympics, which Dunning attributed partly to sponsorship. Supporters point to the proprioceptive-cue explanation and to trials such as those cited above that measure posture directly.[1]

Products differ in width, length, adhesive strength, water resistance and skin sensitivity; the tape is described as latex-free cotton with a heat-activated acrylic adhesive, and manufacturer-style descriptions give wear times of up to about four days.[1] Both pre-cut posture strips and general kinesiology tape rolls are sold under Kinesio, KT Tape and other brand names.

For posture specifically, a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Musculoskeletal Research (Niranjan, Harikesavan and Kalyan) included nine randomized trials with 293 participants with upper-quadrant postural dysfunction. Taping was associated with a significant difference in forward shoulder angle, with no significant difference in craniovertebral angle or pain; the authors cautioned that evidence quality was low.[2]

A 2024 randomized, double-blind trial in Medicine (Demircioglu and Genc) assigned 114 people with rounded shoulder posture and subacromial impingement to Kinesio taping or sham taping. Taping reduced pain, improved proprioception in abduction and improved posture on the New York Posture Rating Chart (P = .040) immediately after application; effects beyond that were not examined.[3]

Reviews of the tape for other purposes include a 2012 finding of trivial pain relief in sports injuries, a 2014 finding of negligible effect on muscle strength, and a 2015 finding of benefit over no treatment, but not over other treatments, for chronic musculoskeletal pain.[1] A 2026 meta-analysis reported significant pain reduction in patellofemoral pain syndrome, while a 2021 review found no strong evidence for pain relief in knee osteoarthritis.[4][5]

Studies of other uses describe a range of results. In 34 soccer players, knee extension force did not differ between Kinesio tape and Micropore tape immediately or 24 hours after application.[6] In a prospective comparative study of 57 analysable ACL reconstruction patients (28 taped, 29 controls), early postoperative pain over three days was assessed and the authors titled the report as showing no benefit for that outcome.[7]

In breast-cancer-related lymphedema, a pilot trial in 41 patients found no significant difference between a Kinesio tape group and a short-stretch bandage group on any outcome, and a single-blind trial of 65 women reported that edema reduction with multilayered bandages was larger than in the taping groups, with no significant difference between real and quasi-tape.[8][9] A randomised study of 30 patients examined tape on swelling, pain and trismus after surgical fixation of zygomatico-maxillary complex fractures.[10]

As with any skin adhesive, skin irritation is a general consideration, and people with sensitive skin sometimes test a small area first. The trials above do not describe adverse effects in detail.[2][3]
